newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London remained within their narrow trading range. Interest in the front spreads formed the focus of market activity as movements on the New York market failed to inspire sentiment in London. October closed 70 points higher at $348.90 a tonne, while December was up 40 points at $344.00.
In New York raw sugar futures ended slightly higher in line with the London white sugar market. However, trade was quiet ahead of the US labour day holiday on Monday which will shut New York markets.

While tenders by both Syria and Egypt this week provided some support, overall demand remains really sluggish. Traders said longer term supplies are seen ample, with Cuban sugar cane plantings reported to be 88 per cent of the July/August plan or 104,250 acres, ahead of last year's 66 per cent of plan. There is still some uncertainty about the European crop, which looks to be lower than last season.

FRANCE - The third sugar beet tests by French producers show a satisfactory increase in root weight after recent rains. The increase reached 12.64 tonnes against 6.80 tonnes last year and the average (1991/95) of 7.43 tonnes. However, the rains led to decrease in sugar content which affected the sugar yield per ha.

As a result the increase in sugar yield per ha was only 1.44 tonnes against 1.54 tonnes last year and the average of 1.68 tonnes. The sugar yield per ha at the end of August reached 7.65 tonnes, 9.6 per cent less than last year and 15 per cent below average. The beet test results of August 12 support our latest production estimate for 1996/97 of roughly 3.9 million tonnes in white value terms.

THAILAND - Thailand exported 340,200 tonnes of sugar, raw value, in July 1996, nearly 20 per cent less than was exported the same month the previous year. That brought total exports since the beginning of 1995/96 up to 4.3 million tonnes, one million tonnes more than was exported the same period in 1994/95. Total exports in crop year 1994/95 (October/September) reached 3.9 million tonnes, up from 2.8 million tonnes exported in 1993/94.

RUSSIA - The 1996/97 Russian sugar beet harvest has begun in some southern beet growing areas (North Caucasus and Central Chernozem). At the end of August 3,000 ha (about 0.3 per cent of total plantings) had been harvested compared to 4,000 ha at the same date last year. Yields were only 19.1 tonnes per ha as against 21.9 tonnes per ha at the same time last year. As yields normally go down during the course of the campaign, average yields for the whole of 1996/97 are now estimated at 15.5 to 16.5 tonnes per ha or around 10 per cent less than last year.

The lower yield expectations reflect lower fertilizer applications and a lower level of other farm inputs. Current indications are that the crop may be lower than had been expected and the overall estimate has been reduced by about 1.2 million tonnes to 16-18 million tonnes or some 11 per cent less than last year. This would be the second lowest output for the last 40 years after the 1993 crop. However, weather still has a crucial role to play so that it will take some time before a clearer picture would emerge.

NORTHERN GERMANY - Beet development is still lagging behind in Northern Germany. According to industry sources, beet weight at the end of August reached 47.9 tonnes per ha, compared to 52.8 tonnes in 1995. Sugar content amounted to 15.66 per cent compared to 15.69 per cent in 1995. This resulted in a theoretical sugar weight of 7.50 tonnes per ha, down from 8.28 tonnes in 1995.

However, due to the rather high number of beets per ha (86,709 units vs 78,900 in 1995) and good leaf weight (599 grams per root vs 508 grams), there still seems to be scope for substantial improvement.

IRELAND - The latest beet rest results of August 30, 1996 show that beet development continues to be rather favourable while sugar content is considerably below last year. Root yield per ha amounted to 45.08 tonnes, 14.16 tonnes more than in the previous test compared to 41.99 tonnes after a rise of 5.13 tonnes in 1995 and the average of 40.42 tonnes.

Sugar content on the other hand showed only a marginal increase of 1.27 percentage points to 13.51 per cent, down from 16.29 per cent in 1995 and the average of 14.19 per cent. This resulted in a theoretical sugar weight of 6.05 tonnes per ha, up 2.32 tonnes on the previous test and against 6.83 tonnes in 1995 and the average of 5.63 tonnes. Given the slightly lower area sown to beet, it is unlikely that Ireland will match last year's excellent results, but nevertheless a very good crop seems to be in prospect.

The state-run Trading Corporation of Pakistan (TCP) said that India had offered to sell it 50,000 tonnes of white sugar at $389 per tonne, c&f, for delivery by September 30. However, the TCP has not yet taken any decision whether to accept the offer or not.
